netperf_runner: fixup error handling for 'None' results We access the 'result.exit_status' field before checking if it's None. That's broken. Reorganize the ignore_failures vs. !ignore_failures logic a bit, and add a new TestFail() condition for when we get no results and haven't asked for 'ignore_failures=True'. BUG=chromium:629137 TEST=network_AttenuatedPerf, with high attenuation (causing association failures on certain boards) Change-Id: I7881391eed3bb10a8b58573e1567a6c3e5aaea0b Signed-off-by: Brian Norris <briannorris@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/696267 Reviewed-by: Harpreet Grewal <harpreet@chromium.org>

netperf: limit extent of retries, timeout delays When run with 'ignore_failures' (e.g., with AttenuatedPerf), we forgive all failure and just wait until the end to collect a None result. This is pointless and time-wasting, especially on attenuated tests, where we ramp up attenuation until the client gets abysmal performance (and likely disconnects from the AP eventually). We should not keep trying to get 10 samples (MEASUREMENT_MAX_SAMPLES) when we see multiple None results (i.e., errors). Limit this to 2 failures, and abort on the 3rd. Also, CL:217970 increased the netperf timeout from a 10 second margin (on top of test time) to 120 seconds, with no explanation. This seems excessively high for a 10-second test. And note that we do hit this timeout sometimes, when running AttenuatedPerf. So let's decrease that to 60 seconds, which should still be conservative, but should save us several times that much on some tests, since netperf sessions often include multiple retries. BUG=none TEST=network_WiFi_AttenuatedPerf Change-Id: I7712fbcb39176c28b037231bb6c4708579672ec4 Signed-off-by: Brian Norris <briannorris@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/696671 Reviewed-by: Harpreet Grewal <harpreet@chromium.org>

UPSTREAM: xhci: fix isoc endpoint dequeue from advancing too far on transaction error Isoc TDs usually consist of one TRB, sometimes two. When all goes well we receive only one success event for a TD, and move the dequeue pointer to the next TD. This fails if the TD consists of two TRBs and we get a transfer error on the first TRB, we will then see two events for that TD. Fix this by making sure the event we get is for the last TRB in that TD before moving the dequeue pointer to the next TD. This will resolve some of the uvc and dvb issues with the "ERROR Transfer event TRB DMA ptr not part of current TD" error message Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> Signed-off-by: Mathias Nyman <mathias.nyman@linux.intel.com> Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org> (cherry picked from commit d104d0152a97fade389f47635b73a9ccc7295d0b) Signed-off-by: Vedang Patel <vedang.patel@intel.com> BUG=b/65911240 TEST=Build the kernel with this patch and deploy to my CFM locally. Run local present for days, also tried plug/unplug cable. It works fine and didn't see the error message. network_WiFi_AttenuatedPerf: autodetect/report max attenuation CL:286195 changed both the min and max attenuation values we would use. This artificially restricted us to a range of +20 dB, which doesn't really cover as much range as we'd like, in some cases. Let's try to bump that back up. However, in testing more extreme attenuation, I've found that at least on some DUTs, we can't even connect to the AP. Our netperf code isn't able to promptly handle this condition, as the current logic tries for 10 samples (or failures), each consisting of up to 3 retries, and a 2 minute timeout. That means it will take 1 hour for a run to complete in the null case where we haven't even associated correctly. We should probably improve the netperf logic to handle this a little better too, but as a first step, we can check for a connection before kicking off a session. So this CL: (a) adds a basic connectivity test for each attenuation level (b) stops testing an attenuation level if any netperf session returns no result (c) logs (and reports to the keyval storage) the maximum attenuation reached (d) expands the theoretical max attenuation to 100dB, instead of "start + 20" Example runs now look something like this: INFO | autoserv| RvR test: current attenuation = 79 dB INFO | autoserv| Waiting for AttenuatedPerf_a_4fgeb_ch1 to reach one of ['ready', 'portal', 'online']... INFO | autoserv| ...ended up in state 'online' (success) after 0.007059 seconds. INFO | autoserv| Pinging from the client. INFO | autoserv| Could not establish connection at 79 dB INFO | autoserv| Error: Ping command failed with code=1 INFO | autoserv| Running time 968.1 seconds. INFO | autoserv| Reached attenuation of: 75 dB (signal -76 dBm) BUG=none TEST=network_WiFi_AttenuatedPerf, see expanded atten values tested Change-Id: Ie435ecc80ac78017dc9f003dd2cf0c4ef446323b Signed-off-by: Brian Norris <briannorris@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/695707 Reviewed-by: Harpreet Grewal <harpreet@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Kirtika Ruchandani <kirtika@chromium.org>

intel_x86: Enable/disable SLP_S0 signal based on S0ix entry/exit Runtime S0ix results in SLP_S0 signal being toggled continuously resulting in an interrupt storm on the EC. In order to avoid this, enable SLP_S0 power signal only when host indicates intent to enter S0ix and disable when host exits from S0ix. BUG=b:65421825 BRANCH=None TEST=Verified that runtime S0ix no longer results in interrupt storm on EC. Normal S0ix works fine on soraka. Verified state of SLP_S0 using powerindebug. Change-Id: I9ca62b8122afd8acedc2c353106407fdcc284925 Signed-off-by: Furquan Shaikh <furquan@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/679982 Reviewed-by: Aaron Durbin <adurbin@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Shawn N <shawnn@chromium.org>

FROMLIST: Input: elan_i2c - do not clobber interrupt trigger on x86 On x86 we historically used falling edge interrupts in the driver because that's how first Chrome devices were configured. They also did not use ACPI to enumerate I2C devices (because back then there was no kernel support for that), so trigger was hard-coded in the driver. However the controller behavior is much more reliable if we use level triggers, and that is how we configured ARM devices, and how want to configure newer x86 devices as well. All newer x86 boxes have their I2C devices enumerated in ACPI. Let's see if platform code (ACPI, DT) described interrupt and specified particular trigger type, and if so, let's use it instead of always clobbering trigger with IRQF_TRIGGER_FALLING. We will still use this trigger type as a fallback if platform code left interrupt trigger unconfigured. Bugzilla: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=196761 Signed-off-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dmitry.torokhov@gmail.com> BUG=b:66163187 TEST=Build and boot on kahlee, make sure touchpad works (am from https://patchwork.kernel.org/patch/9976411/) Signed-off-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dtor@chromium.org> Change-Id: I99ac8dc2fe805fa698d481f30848cebdb3cc50b0 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/690576 Tested-by: Aaron Durbin <adurbin@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Guenter Roeck <groeck@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Aaron Durbin <adurbin@chromium.org>
